chunks: "Start from Z 0 equals square root of (R plus j omega L) over (G plus j omega C) with everything per unit length.
At high frequency, where omega L much greater than R and omega C much greater than G , it collapses to square root of L over C .
So more inductance raises the impedance, more capacitance lowers it, and I can think of every layout change as changing one of those.
A wider trace, or a trace closer to its plane, adds capacitance and removes inductance, so Z 0 drops. A thicker dielectric, or a narrower trace, does the opposite.
A higher dielectric constant raises C so Z 0 falls by one over root epsilon. R and G are really about loss.
At high frequency they add a small imaginary part and attenuate the signal: series resistance, with skin effect, and dielectric loss.
At low frequency, below roughly where R equals omega L , the resistance dominates and Z 0 gets bigger and complex.
On a fine PCB trace that corner is a megahertz or two; on a coax it's tens of kilohertz.

Microstrip versus coax: coax has the field entirely inside a uniform dielectric between the centre conductor and the shield, so Z 0 equals (60 over square root of r ) log (D over d) and it is shielded and non-dispersive.
Microstrip has its field partly in the board and partly in the air above, so I use an effective dielectric constant, around 3.
2 on FR-4, only approximate formulas, and it's open, so it radiates, couples to neighbours and is slightly dispersive."
